title: George Lewis Fowler Sr.
summary: George Lewis Fowler Sr. (circa 1858–1931) was a Montaukett gardener, caretaker, and gondolier whose Freetown home preserves a family history of labor, dispossession, and continuity after Indian Fields.
content:
George Lewis Fowler Sr. (circa 1858–1931) was a Montaukett gardener, caretaker, and gondolier whose life connected Indian Fields at Montauk with Freetown in East Hampton. His story documents family continuity through dispossession, skilled labor, and the preservation of a modest home that later became an important place for interpreting Montaukett history.1

Family life at Indian Fields

Fowler was born around 1858 at Indian Fields, the reserved Montaukett homeland at Montauk. Records place him there with his parents and younger brothers in the 1880 census, working as an “odd job” laborer. He later married Sarah Melissa Horton, also recorded as Melissa Horton; profiles of their children identify both parents as Montaukett. The reviewed sources do not provide Sarah’s verified birth or death dates, parents, independent occupation, or a confirmed portrait, so this article does not infer those details. Their household belonged to a wider Montaukett family network that continued across Montauk, Freetown, and neighboring East End communities.2

The 1885 Benson agreement

On April 21, 1885, Fowler, his sister Maria Pharaoh, and Maria’s son Wyandanch Pharaoh signed an agreement with developer Arthur W. Benson. The agreement offered Fowler $100 and land in Freetown while requiring the family to give up residence at Indian Fields. The document belongs to a larger process that displaced Montaukett families from their homeland; describing it as an ordinary sale would hide the unequal pressure surrounding it.3

Gardening, care work, and the East Hampton economy

In East Hampton, Fowler worked as a gardener and gondolier for artist Thomas Moran, rowing Moran’s imported gondola on Hook Pond. He also cared for the historic Home, Sweet Home property. These jobs place Montaukett labor inside the landscapes and institutions now associated with East Hampton’s public history. Fowler’s work supported his family while maintaining a Montaukett presence after removal from Indian Fields.4

A house rebuilt in Freetown

Older accounts often said that Fowler’s house was moved intact from Indian Fields to Freetown. Architectural and archaeological research supports a more careful conclusion: materials from Montauk may have been reused, but the surviving house was probably built or substantially reconstructed at its Freetown location around 1885. The distinction matters because the house records both forced movement and the family’s work of rebuilding a home.5

Reading the family photographs carefully

Around 1910, Fowler was photographed with Anthony Beaman and Eliza Fowler Beaman. Captions reproduced in The History and Archaeology of the Montauk disagree about Eliza’s relationship to George, describing her in one place as a granddaughter and in another as a daughter. This biography preserves that conflict rather than choosing a relationship the cited record does not resolve.6

Keeping the house in the family

In his 1931 will, Fowler left the Freetown house to his son Norris and directed that it not be sold during Norris’s lifetime. He also protected another son’s right to live there. The provision made the house more than surviving building fabric: it was a deliberate family anchor after the loss of Indian Fields.7

Reading the map

The two map stops connect Indian Fields and the Fowler House in date order. The line is a learning chronology, not a reconstruction of Fowler’s exact route or a claim about a precise private residence at Montauk.

why_this_matters: George Lewis Fowler’s life shifts attention from a historic building alone to the Montaukett family who rebuilt life around it. His work and his effort to keep the Freetown house in the family show continuity, agency, and care after dispossession from Indian Fields.
activity_update_summary: Clarified what the surviving sources do and do not document about Sarah Melissa Horton Fowler without creating a speculative standalone biography.
